screens.title: Consolidating Predictive, Passive, and Active Data
screens.narratorSegment: Consolidation is the first critical step after data collection. It means bringing the predictive design, passive RSSI and SNR samples, noise floor measurements, and active throughput and retransmission tests onto one floor plan so you can compare them directly. Start by importing the predictive model and overlaying passive walk data; then add active test traces. The goal is to identify agreements and discrepancies, for example where a predictive model shows good coverage but passive measurements reveal high noise, or where passive RSSI looks healthy yet active throughput is poor. Those mismatches point to different root causes: high noise suggests interference and invites spectrum analysis, while throughput problems with good RSSI point to capacity or retransmission issues. When you consolidate, maintain metadata: timestamps, device IDs, channel info, and test configurations. This traceability lets you map a finding back to the measurement that supports it. A common misconception is to base recommendations on a single layer; always cross‑check across the three data types. After consolidation, mark candidate problem zones for focused heatmap generation and targeted corrective actions. How confident are you that every recommendation references at least two data sources?

keyIdea.text: Merging predictive, passive, and active layers exposes root causes so recommendations address the real problem, not a symptom.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Consolidate Data
Process

Merge layers and preserve traceability

1. Import predictive plan and baseline AP placements.
2. Overlay passive walk samples: RSSI, SNR, noise floor, channel observations.
3. Add active traces: throughput, retransmissions, and roaming latency.
4. Tag data with timestamps, device IDs and channel info for auditing.
Supporting explanation
  • Cross‑check: a finding should be visible in at least two data layers when possible.
  • Discrepancy example: good RSSI but high noise floor suggests interference, not weak coverage.
  • Active vs passive: throughput problems with good RSSI often indicate capacity limits or high retransmissions.
Example scenario
A predictive map showed -65 dBm coverage in a conference area. Passive walk found -60 dBm RSSI but an elevated noise floor. Active tests measured throughput collapse under load. Consolidation revealed interference during business hours causing low SNR and high retransmissions.
Key Takeaway
Do not act on one measurement alone. Consolidate layers so recommendations solve root causes.

screens.title: Heatmaps: What Each Type Reveals
screens.narratorSegment: Heatmaps are visual overlays that make RF data legible across a floor plan. Each type answers a specific question. A coverage heatmap (RSSI) answers where the minimum signal level is met and reveals coverage gaps or over‑powered zones. An SNR heatmap reveals signal quality and shows where noise or interference reduces usable performance even if RSSI is strong. Capacity heatmaps use throughput and client density to show where the network can support demand; these are essential for meeting rooms and auditoriums. Interference heatmaps indicate co‑channel and adjacent‑channel congestion, pointing to where the channel plan needs adjustment or mitigation is required. Roaming heatmaps show where handoffs are expected and where clients may stick to an AP too long. When you generate heatmaps, switch between them and look for patterns: a coverage gap that matches low capacity is different from good coverage with low capacity. A common mistake is to present only the coverage map to stakeholders; that obscures quality and capacity issues. Always include the heatmap type in your report and explain its operational implication so the business can accept the recommended change with confidence.

keyIdea.text: Coverage shows where signal exists; SNR shows quality; capacity shows ability to serve clients; interference shows congestion; roaming shows handoff behavior.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Heatmaps

Heatmap types and interpretations

Coverage (RSSI)
Shows where minimum signal thresholds are met. Look for red zones under target and areas of excessive overlap.
SNR
Shows signal quality. Low SNR with good RSSI indicates noise or interference reducing usable throughput.
Capacity
Maps throughput and client density to reveal bottlenecks in high‑demand areas.
Interference
Highlights CCI and ACI so you can refine channel plans or mitigate non‑Wi‑Fi sources.
Practical tip
Always include at least two heatmaps when recommending a change: one showing the symptom and one showing the likely root cause. That makes your recommendation defensible to non‑technical stakeholders.
Example: mixed symptom
If coverage map shows good RSSI but SNR heatmap shows low values in the same area, the problem is noise. Your next step is a spectrum or interference analysis and a recommendation that addresses the interference source rather than adding APs.
Key Takeaway
Match the heatmap to the question you need to answer and present paired visuals to justify each recommendation.

screens.title: Coverage vs SNR: Why Both Matter
screens.narratorSegment: Coverage and SNR answers are related but distinct, and mixing them up leads to poor recommendations. Coverage heatmaps report RSSI — where the signal level meets a target. SNR heatmaps show the ratio between signal and background noise and are the better indicator of usable throughput. A common real‑world case is excellent RSSI but low SNR; this indicates a noisy environment where clients still see a strong transmitter but cannot extract data reliably. The correct action in that case is not simply to add more APs, which can worsen co‑channel interference, but to identify and mitigate noise sources, change channel plan or adjust power. Conversely, a weak RSSI with adequate SNR implies the signal is too low — here moving or adding an AP or increasing power in a controlled way helps. A misconception is to always reach for more APs. More APs without addressing SNR or channel assignment can increase retransmissions and reduce aggregate capacity. When you produce a report, show both coverage and SNR heatmaps side by side and explain the operational implication for each area of concern. How would you justify adding an AP versus investigating interference?

keyIdea.text: High RSSI is not sufficient; SNR determines whether that signal can be used effectively. Use both maps to choose the right corrective action.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Coverage vs SNR
Coverage (RSSI)
Indicates where signal level meets a threshold. Useful to spot dead zones but not alone sufficient to guarantee performance.
Example: Office area shows -60 dBm across desks — good coverage baseline.
Common mistake
Adding APs when RSSI looks fine can increase co‑channel interference if SNR and channel plan are not considered.
SNR (Signal-to-Noise Ratio)
Measures signal quality. Low SNR reduces throughput regardless of RSSI. Investigate noise sources before adding APs.
Example: Conference room shows -55 dBm RSSI but SNR of 12 dB and throughput collapse under load — likely non‑Wi‑Fi noise or heavy CCI.
Key Takeaway
Always present both coverage and SNR heatmaps and explain the root cause before recommending AP additions.

screens.title: Capacity and Interference Heatmaps
screens.narratorSegment: Capacity and interference heatmaps answer operational questions about performance under load. A capacity heatmap uses active throughput and client density to show where the network meets or fails to meet expected service levels; these maps are essential for high‑density rooms where many devices compete for airtime. Interference heatmaps highlight co‑channel and adjacent‑channel problems as well as non‑Wi‑Fi noise sources. Use them together: if capacity is low in a zone, check interference heatmaps to determine whether CCI or ACI is the cause. If interference is high, changing the channel plan or lowering transmit power to shrink cells may help. For capacity issues with low interference, adding APs or changing antenna types can increase available airtime — but only after ensuring channel reuse and power are properly tuned. A common misconception is that capacity issues are always solved by adding more APs; if interference or poor roaming behavior is present, more APs can worsen the situation. In your analysis, always list which heatmap drove each recommendation and quantify the expected effect where possible, for example expected throughput improvement or reduced retransmission percentage.

keyIdea.text: Capacity gaps require either more airtime or less interference. Diagnose which before changing AP count or power.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Capacity & Interference
Capacity heatmap
Maps throughput and client density so you can see whether the network supports expected loads. Use active tests that simulate concurrent clients where possible.
Example: Large meeting room throughput drops to 20–30 Mbps with 10+ devices — capacity shortfall that needs design changes.
Action prompt
If capacity fails, quantify whether additional APs or airtime management are the correct response after checking interference.
Interference heatmap
Shows CCI/ACI and non‑Wi‑Fi noise. High interference in a zone suggests changing channels, adjusting power, or mitigating non‑Wi‑Fi devices.
Example: Three APs in a meeting room all on the same 5 GHz channel at -60 dBm — adjust channel plan and consider power or antenna changes.
Key Takeaway
Combine capacity and interference maps to choose whether to add APs, change power, or reassign channels; document which map motivated the decision.

screens.title: Formulating Actionable Recommendations
screens.narratorSegment: Actionable recommendations are the heart of your report. A recommendation must be specific, justified by data, and state expected benefit and risk. Start with a short summary line such as 'Relocate AP‑A 2 meters east to reduce wall attenuation in conference room C' followed by the justification — reference the coverage and SNR heatmaps and active throughput tests. Prioritize fixes with clear impact: safety or uptime first, then high‑impact performance issues. Typical recommendations include AP relocation, adding or removing APs to correct over‑ or under‑design, adjusting transmit power to balance coverage and capacity, refining the channel plan to reduce CCI/ACI, selecting directional antennas in hallways, and identifying non‑Wi‑Fi interference sources for mitigation. When possible, include measurable targets — for example expected RSSI improvement or reduced retransmission percentage — so stakeholders can verify success. A common error is vague recommendations like 'optimize channels' without stating which APs and which channels. Always map each recommendation to the heatmap or data that supports it, and include a cost or BoM note if hardware changes are required. That traceability makes your recommendations implementable and auditable.

keyIdea.title: Recommendations must be specific and traceable
keyIdea.text: Each recommendation should cite the supporting measurement, describe the action, and state the expected outcome so it can be validated.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Recommendations

Recommendation pattern

Action: Clear, specific change to make.
Justification: Which heatmap or measurement motivates this action.
Expected outcome: Measurable improvement and risk notes.
Examples
  • AP Relocation: move AP X 2 m to avoid concrete column — expect RSSI +5 dB in affected area.
  • Channel Plan: reassign three meeting room APs to non‑overlapping 5 GHz channels to reduce CCI.
  • Power Tuning: lower transmit power in open office to reduce cell overlap and improve capacity.
Prioritization
Rank fixes by impact and effort. Quick low‑effort wins first, then planned changes requiring procurement.
Key Takeaway
Make each recommendation actionable, measurable, and tied to survey evidence so implementation succeeds.

screens.title: Assembling the Site Survey Report and BoM
screens.narratorSegment: The site survey report is your deliverable — it must communicate findings clearly to both technical and non‑technical stakeholders. A recommended structure begins with an Executive Summary that states key findings and recommended actions in plain language. Follow with an Introduction describing scope and methodology so readers understand how data was collected. Reiterate Requirements so the reader can connect findings to agreed goals. Include a Current State Analysis if relevant, then the Survey Findings with heatmaps and annotated problem areas. Next, Recommendations: list prioritized, justified actions and reference the supporting heatmaps. The Proposed Design section contains final AP placement maps, channel plan, and configuration guidance. The BoM lists hardware, antennas, cables and licenses with quantities and notes on alternatives. Appendices hold raw data exports, additional heatmaps, and photos. Tailor the language and level of detail: executives need the big picture and cost; engineers need configs and raw data. Common mistakes include burying recommendations in appendices or presenting raw charts without interpretation. A concise, well-structured report increases the chance that your recommended changes will be funded and implemented. Assembling the Site Survey Report and BoM means use an executive summary, findings with heatmaps, prioritized recommendations, proposed design, and a clear bom so stakeholders can decide and implement.. In practical terms, a clear structure for technical and executive audiences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Report & BoM

Report structure

1. Executive Summary — high level findings and recommended next steps for decision makers.
2. Introduction — scope and methodology so readers know how data was produced.
3. Requirements Review — restate business and technical goals to align solutions.
4. Survey Findings — heatmaps and annotated problem areas with data citations.
5. Recommendations & Proposed Design — prioritized, actionable steps and final AP map.
Bill of Materials (BoM)
List all hardware and software by quantity and model, and include notes for alternatives. This helps procurement and budgeting and prevents delays during implementation.
Appendices
Attach raw data, additional heatmaps and photos for auditors and engineers who need detail beyond the main report.
Key Takeaway
Make the report readable at two levels: clear summary for decision makers and detailed evidence for implementers.

screens.title: Common Reporting Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Reports fail when they are either too raw or too vague. Presenting raw logs and heatmaps without interpretation leaves stakeholders guessing; giving recommendations without citing evidence leaves them unjustified. Avoid overly technical language in the executive summary — executives need the impact and the cost. For engineers, include appendices with raw datasets and test parameters so changes can be validated. Common mistakes include recommending AP additions without addressing interference, burying the BoM in an appendix where procurement may miss it, and failing to prioritize fixes. Fix these by pairing every recommendation with the supporting heatmap or measurement, stating the expected measurable benefit, and adding a priority and estimated effort. Also, include a short implementation note that flags risks and required downtime if any. A helpful structure is: symptom, evidence, recommendation, expected result, and risk. This makes reviews faster and approvals more likely, and prevents rework that comes from ambiguous guidance. How will you structure your next report to avoid these pitfalls? Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Reporting Mistakes

Frequent errors

  • Present raw data without interpretation for stakeholders.
  • Recommend actions without citing the supporting measurement.
  • Bury the BoM where procurement cannot find it easily.
Corrective checklist
- Pair symptom with the heatmap and the active test evidence.
- State expected improvement and implementation risk.
- Prioritize and estimate effort so stakeholders can decide quickly.
Example
Rather than saying 'optimize channels', show the interference heatmap, list specific AP IDs and their current channels, and recommend the new channels with expected reduction in CCI.
Key Takeaway
Clarity and traceability in reports reduce implementation risk and speed approvals.

screens.title: Continuous Monitoring and Re‑surveying
screens.narratorSegment: WLANs live in dynamic environments. Occupant changes, remodeled spaces, new neighboring networks, or new devices can alter RF behavior, so monitoring and periodic re‑surveys are vital. Establish monitoring thresholds and triggers such as sudden increases in retransmissions, persistent coverage complaints in a previously green zone, or a measurable drop in aggregate throughput. When a trigger occurs, perform targeted checks: a quick passive walk, spectrum scan, and focused active tests in the affected zone. Use those findings to decide whether a full re‑survey is required or a local fix suffices. Document monitoring results and add them to the operations runbook so staff can correlate incidents and interventions. Continuous monitoring also provides data for capacity planning: trends in client density and throughput indicate when upgrades or design changes will be needed. A common misconception is that a site survey is a one‑time task; instead, treat it as an iterative process where monitoring informs future surveys. In your report, include a recommended monitoring cadence and the re‑survey triggers you used so the client can maintain long‑term performance. Continuous Monitoring and Re‑surveying means define monitoring thresholds and re‑survey triggers so the wlan adapts to changes and long‑term performance is preserved.. In practical terms, when to re‑survey and how monitoring informs lifecycle maintenance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Monitoring & Re‑survey

Monitoring triggers

- Persistent user complaints in a previously healthy area.
- Spike in retransmission or retry rates.
- Sudden throughput degradation or roaming failures.
Re‑survey approach
Begin with targeted passive and spectrum scans, then expand to active tests. Document changes and update the floor plan and BoM as needed.
Operations note
Include monitoring cadence and re‑survey criteria in the report to hand over to operations staff.
Key Takeaway
Treat surveys as part of a lifecycle: monitor, trigger, investigate, and re‑survey when evidence supports it.

screens.title: Activity: Develop Recommendations from Survey Findings
screens.narratorSegment: Now apply what you’ve learned to the provided scenario. You have predictive coverage that looked good with 15 APs, but passive data shows three large meeting rooms with multiple APs on the same 5 GHz channel and a neighboring strong 2.4 GHz network affecting perimeter offices. Active tests show meeting room throughput collapses under 10+ devices and retransmissions spike. Your task is to create at least three concrete recommendations. Use the rule: symptom, evidence, recommendation, and expected outcome. For the meeting rooms, the symptom is low throughput and high retransmissions; the evidence is active tests and interference heatmaps showing three APs on Ch36. A recommended action is to reassign channels on those APs, adjust transmit power to reduce overlap, and consider adding capacity‑oriented APs or directional antennas to serve each room. For perimeter offices on 2.4 GHz, recommend moving clients to 5 GHz where possible, change 2.4 GHz channels to avoid strong neighbor channels, or recommend shielding/coordination with the neighboring business. For general optimization, evaluate whether the original 15 APs caused over‑design and whether some APs should be removed or power‑tuned to reduce CCI. In your report, include the heatmaps and expected measurable benefits such as throughput recovery targets and reduced retransmission rates.

keyIdea.text: Use evidence from predictive, passive and active data to produce prioritized, measurable recommendations for meeting rooms, perimeter interference, and general optimization.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Activity: Recommendations

Scenario recap

Predictive design: 15 APs with -65 dBm target. Passive: good noise floor overall, but three meeting rooms show multiple APs on the same 5 GHz channel. Neighbor strong on 2.4 GHz channels 1 and 6. Active: meeting rooms throughput drops to 20–30 Mbps with 10+ devices and retransmissions spike to 25–30%.
Recommended actions (example)
  1. Meeting rooms: Reassign the three APs to non‑overlapping 5 GHz channels, lower transmit power to reduce overlap, and consider adding capacity APs or directional antennas to isolate each room. Expected result: throughput recovery and lower retransmissions.
  2. Perimeter 2.4 GHz interference: Move capable clients to 5 GHz via band steering, change 2.4 GHz channels away from neighbor overlap, and investigate neighbor coordination or shielding. Expected result: reduced intermittent connectivity.
  3. General optimization: Review whether 15 APs cause over‑design. Remove or power‑tune APs in over‑lapped zones to reduce co‑channel interference and improve overall capacity distribution.
Checklist
Attach heatmaps showing channel overlap, SNR and active throughput; list AP IDs and channels; include BoM changes if new APs or antennas are required.
Key Takeaway
Make each recommendation measurable and reference the data that motivated it so validation is straightforward after implementation.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's lock in the essential concepts. Post‑survey analysis is the interpretation of measured data to find root causes and guide fixes. A site survey report packages those findings, prioritized recommendations, and a Bill of Materials so stakeholders can act. Actionable recommendations are specific, justified by data, and measurable. Coverage maps show where signal levels meet targets; SNR maps reveal usable quality; capacity maps indicate whether the network supports expected client density; interference maps show CCI/ACI and non‑Wi‑Fi noise. Continuous monitoring with defined triggers keeps the WLAN healthy and informs when to re‑survey. Remember: present paired evidence for each recommendation and prioritize by impact and effort. This approach turns measurements into well‑justified decisions that improve user experience and reduce rework. Module 5 › Chapter 5.6 › Quick Reference
Coverage Map

Capacity Map
Visualizes throughput and client density to reveal bottlenecks.

fullNarratorScript:
This lesson takes you from collected measurements to decisions you can present and defend. After a predictive design and both passive and active walks, the core value comes from consolidating those layers, spotting mismatches, and using heatmaps to tell a clear technical and business story. You will learn how to interpret coverage, SNR, capacity, interference, and roaming overlays and then translate them into concrete recommendations such as AP relocation, power changes, channel plan updates, or antenna swaps. A professional report organizes those findings into an executive summary, detailed survey results, proposed design, and a Bill of Materials so stakeholders can act. For example, if passive data shows strong RSSI but active tests reveal low throughput, you will learn to diagnose capacity bottlenecks versus interference and write recommendations that explain why a change is needed. Finally, we’ll cover continuous monitoring and when to re‑survey so the WLAN endures changes in occupancy and neighboring networks. Keep this practical mindset: data must lead to justified actions the client can implement.

By the end of these screens you will consolidate survey data, read and generate heatmaps, and write recommendations that fix measured problems. First, you will learn to merge predictive designs with passive and active survey layers so every decision is grounded in measurements. Second, you will generate and interpret heatmaps for coverage, SNR, capacity, interference, and roaming to reveal hidden problems. Third, you will translate findings into actionable recommendations such as AP relocation, power tuning, channel plan changes, and antenna selection. Fourth, you will draft a clear site survey report and a Bill of Materials so stakeholders can review costs and approve work. Each objective emphasizes both the technical skill and why it matters: stakeholders need concise evidence and justifications to implement changes. Expect hands‑on practice where you make three concrete recommendations from a summarized survey case. Keep these goals in mind as we move through consolidation, heatmap interpretation, recommendation formulation, and report writing.

These additional objectives focus on sustained WLAN health and making your work actionable in the real world. You will learn how to create recommendations that are directly traceable to measured problems, including how to justify AP moves, power changes, and channel plan revisions. You will also practice developing a clear Bill of Materials listing hardware and licenses so procurement and budgeting are straightforward. Finally, you will plan for continuous monitoring and define re‑survey triggers so that your WLAN adapts to occupancy changes, remodeling, or new interference. In practice, these skills mean the difference between a one‑off report and a living design: you give operations a roadmap to keep the network healthy. Each objective includes a small visual mnemonic to help you remember whether a document is technical, executive, or procurement facing.

Consolidation is the first critical step after data collection. It means bringing the predictive design, passive RSSI and SNR samples, noise floor measurements, and active throughput and retransmission tests onto one floor plan so you can compare them directly. Start by importing the predictive model and overlaying passive walk data; then add active test traces. The goal is to identify agreements and discrepancies, for example where a predictive model shows good coverage but passive measurements reveal high noise, or where passive RSSI looks healthy yet active throughput is poor. Those mismatches point to different root causes: high noise suggests interference and invites spectrum analysis, while throughput problems with good RSSI point to capacity or retransmission issues. When you consolidate, maintain metadata: timestamps, device IDs, channel info, and test configurations. This traceability lets you map a finding back to the measurement that supports it. A common misconception is to base recommendations on a single layer; always cross‑check across the three data types. After consolidation, mark candidate problem zones for focused heatmap generation and targeted corrective actions. How confident are you that every recommendation references at least two data sources?

Heatmaps are visual overlays that make RF data legible across a floor plan. Each type answers a specific question. A coverage heatmap (RSSI) answers where the minimum signal level is met and reveals coverage gaps or over‑powered zones. An SNR heatmap reveals signal quality and shows where noise or interference reduces usable performance even if RSSI is strong. Capacity heatmaps use throughput and client density to show where the network can support demand; these are essential for meeting rooms and auditoriums. Interference heatmaps indicate co‑channel and adjacent‑channel congestion, pointing to where the channel plan needs adjustment or mitigation is required. Roaming heatmaps show where handoffs are expected and where clients may stick to an AP too long. When you generate heatmaps, switch between them and look for patterns: a coverage gap that matches low capacity is different from good coverage with low capacity. A common mistake is to present only the coverage map to stakeholders; that obscures quality and capacity issues. Always include the heatmap type in your report and explain its operational implication so the business can accept the recommended change with confidence.

Coverage and SNR answers are related but distinct, and mixing them up leads to poor recommendations. Coverage heatmaps report RSSI — where the signal level meets a target. SNR heatmaps show the ratio between signal and background noise and are the better indicator of usable throughput. A common real‑world case is excellent RSSI but low SNR; this indicates a noisy environment where clients still see a strong transmitter but cannot extract data reliably. The correct action in that case is not simply to add more APs, which can worsen co‑channel interference, but to identify and mitigate noise sources, change channel plan or adjust power. Conversely, a weak RSSI with adequate SNR implies the signal is too low — here moving or adding an AP or increasing power in a controlled way helps. A misconception is to always reach for more APs. More APs without addressing SNR or channel assignment can increase retransmissions and reduce aggregate capacity. When you produce a report, show both coverage and SNR heatmaps side by side and explain the operational implication for each area of concern. How would you justify adding an AP versus investigating interference?

Capacity and interference heatmaps answer operational questions about performance under load. A capacity heatmap uses active throughput and client density to show where the network meets or fails to meet expected service levels; these maps are essential for high‑density rooms where many devices compete for airtime. Interference heatmaps highlight co‑channel and adjacent‑channel problems as well as non‑Wi‑Fi noise sources. Use them together: if capacity is low in a zone, check interference heatmaps to determine whether CCI or ACI is the cause. If interference is high, changing the channel plan or lowering transmit power to shrink cells may help. For capacity issues with low interference, adding APs or changing antenna types can increase available airtime — but only after ensuring channel reuse and power are properly tuned. A common misconception is that capacity issues are always solved by adding more APs; if interference or poor roaming behavior is present, more APs can worsen the situation. In your analysis, always list which heatmap drove each recommendation and quantify the expected effect where possible, for example expected throughput improvement or reduced retransmission percentage.

Actionable recommendations are the heart of your report. A recommendation must be specific, justified by data, and state expected benefit and risk. Start with a short summary line such as 'Relocate AP‑A 2 meters east to reduce wall attenuation in conference room C' followed by the justification — reference the coverage and SNR heatmaps and active throughput tests. Prioritize fixes with clear impact: safety or uptime first, then high‑impact performance issues. Typical recommendations include AP relocation, adding or removing APs to correct over‑ or under‑design, adjusting transmit power to balance coverage and capacity, refining the channel plan to reduce CCI/ACI, selecting directional antennas in hallways, and identifying non‑Wi‑Fi interference sources for mitigation. When possible, include measurable targets — for example expected RSSI improvement or reduced retransmission percentage — so stakeholders can verify success. A common error is vague recommendations like 'optimize channels' without stating which APs and which channels. Always map each recommendation to the heatmap or data that supports it, and include a cost or BoM note if hardware changes are required. That traceability makes your recommendations implementable and auditable.

The site survey report is your deliverable — it must communicate findings clearly to both technical and non‑technical stakeholders. A recommended structure begins with an Executive Summary that states key findings and recommended actions in plain language. Follow with an Introduction describing scope and methodology so readers understand how data was collected. Reiterate Requirements so the reader can connect findings to agreed goals. Include a Current State Analysis if relevant, then the Survey Findings with heatmaps and annotated problem areas. Next, Recommendations: list prioritized, justified actions and reference the supporting heatmaps. The Proposed Design section contains final AP placement maps, channel plan, and configuration guidance. The BoM lists hardware, antennas, cables and licenses with quantities and notes on alternatives. Appendices hold raw data exports, additional heatmaps, and photos. Tailor the language and level of detail: executives need the big picture and cost; engineers need configs and raw data. Common mistakes include burying recommendations in appendices or presenting raw charts without interpretation. A concise, well-structured report increases the chance that your recommended changes will be funded and implemented. Assembling the Site Survey Report and BoM means use an executive summary, findings with heatmaps, prioritized recommendations, proposed design, and a clear bom so stakeholders can decide and implement.. In practical terms, a clear structure for technical and executive audiences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Reports fail when they are either too raw or too vague. Presenting raw logs and heatmaps without interpretation leaves stakeholders guessing; giving recommendations without citing evidence leaves them unjustified. Avoid overly technical language in the executive summary — executives need the impact and the cost. For engineers, include appendices with raw datasets and test parameters so changes can be validated. Common mistakes include recommending AP additions without addressing interference, burying the BoM in an appendix where procurement may miss it, and failing to prioritize fixes. Fix these by pairing every recommendation with the supporting heatmap or measurement, stating the expected measurable benefit, and adding a priority and estimated effort. Also, include a short implementation note that flags risks and required downtime if any. A helpful structure is: symptom, evidence, recommendation, expected result, and risk. This makes reviews faster and approvals more likely, and prevents rework that comes from ambiguous guidance. How will you structure your next report to avoid these pitfalls?
